terms.definition: The ticker of Apple. One of the ten stocks in the track's recorded runs; the chapters' tables and lab outputs use it as a row label.
An experiment that removes one component (a context block, a tool, a rule) and measures what the system loses without it. If nothing drops, the component is not earning its cost.

The judge's honest "unknown", for when the evidence cannot decide. The verdict type is binary, so in week 3 an abstain is stored as fail with an explanation that starts unknown:, and that prefix lets the agreement check leave abstains out of Cohen's kappa and count them instead.
Architecture decision record: one short file per decision, with its context, the decision and its consequences. The track numbers them (ADR-003, ADR-011) and keeps them in the repo.

A program in which the model decides the next step: the code calls the model, runs the tool requests it returns, and calls it again until a reply asks for nothing. A workflow, by contrast, fixes the steps in code.
A benchmark and method for checking whether the source an answer cites actually supports it (Gao et al. 2023). Week 6 cites it for its citation-accuracy eval.
The ticker of Amazon. One of the ten stocks in the track's recorded runs; the chapters' tables and lab outputs use it as a row label.
Attack success rate: the share of injection attempts that change what the model does. A defence should lower it without raising the false-refusal rate.

Average true range: how far a stock's price typically moves in one day, in dollars, averaged over the last 14 days. The track measures distances in ATRs so that a move means the same thing on a $30 stock and a $300 stock.
terms.example: A stock with ATR 4 that closes $8 above its 200-day average sits 2 ATRs above it.

terms.definition: How far past the next price level a target may sit: half the 14-day ATR. It lets a target sit just beyond a level without failing the P4 check.
terms.example: Next level above the entry 105, ATR 4: the target may sit at most at 105 + 0.5 x 4 = 107.

terms.definition: The second step of error analysis: group your open-coding notes into failure classes and count how many outputs fall in each.
One row of price data for a fixed time span: the open, high, low and close prices and the volume traded. A daily bar covers one trading session; a minute bar covers one minute.
A provider endpoint that takes many requests at once and returns the answers later, often within a day, at a lower price. It suits work nobody waits for, such as grading closed theses.
A classic keyword search score: a passage ranks higher when it contains the query's rarer words, more often, in a shorter text. Week 6 compares it with dense (embedding) search.
A move of the price through a level it had not crossed recently, such as a close above the 20-day high, read as the possible start of a trend. breakout_20d is the name of a setup.
The question of whether the next gain comes from the system (prompts, context, tools, checks) or from changing the model's weights. The track answers it with evals before any fine-tuning.
The extra price a provider charges to store a prompt prefix in its cache, above the normal input price. Later reads of the cached prefix cost far less, so caching pays only when the prefix is reused.
terms.example: Sonnet 5.5 per million input tokens: $2.00 normal, $2.50 to write a 5-minute cache, $4.00 for a 1-hour cache, $0.10 to read it.

terms.definition: The two limits on one judge call in week 3. Output tokens: ADR-003 sets 4000, about eight times what a trade is expected to take, so a runaway reply stops but a long reasoning still reaches its verdict. Dollars: before sending, the budget estimates the call's worst case from the model's price row and raises BudgetExceeded if it does not fit, so nothing is sent and nothing is spent.

gigai-core's exception for "there is no score to store". A grader raises it instead of recording a fail: for output that did not parse (week 1), a judge reply with no usable verdict or a thesis the judge may not take (week 3), or a section no claim cites (week 5). Nothing is stored. It is not a fail and not an abstain, and a call that was made is still paid for.
terms.example: A judge reply with no JSON object raises CannotGrade naming what was missing, and the trade gets no verdict.

terms.definition: Two senses in the track. In week 1, a claim rejected only because a claim it derives from was rejected (bad_derivation): the cascade tag marks it, and it is not a failure class of its own. In week 8, a form of model routing that tries a cheap model first and sends the request to a stronger model only when the answer fails a check.
The ticker of Caterpillar. One of the ten stocks in the track's recorded runs; the chapters' tables and lab outputs use it as a row label.
Comparing prices rounded to 2 decimals, the way the model quotes them, instead of the raw stored floats.
terms.example: A level stored as 343.40978 and an entry of 343.41 are equal at cents, so the level is ignored.

terms.definition: Running the current rules (the champion) and one changed rule (the challenger) side by side on the same inputs, and adopting the change only if it wins by a rule fixed in advance, as in an A/B test.
Cutting documents into passages small enough to rank and to paste into a prompt. Where the cut falls decides whether a number stays next to its label.
The code that accepts or rejects one claim of the model's analysis, with a reason, for example a number that matches no source.
The label on every claim the model writes: fact (a number from the source table), inference (a conclusion drawn from other claims) or opinion. Each tag has its own rules for what it may cite.

The last traded price of a session, also called the closing price. The track computes its indicators after the US market closes, from each session's bar: the close, plus the high, low and volume for ATR, levels and rel_volume.

A way to get a confidence interval when items are not independent: resample whole clusters (all the days of one ticker, or one session) with replacement and recompute the statistic many times. The spread of the results is the interval.
A grader that is a deterministic assertion over the parsed reply, so it costs nothing to run and gives the same answer every time.
How often two raters agree beyond what chance alone would give: 1 is perfect, 0 is chance level. The track uses it to measure how well an LLM judge matches your hand labels.
terms.example: 7 of 10 labels agree and chance alone gives 0.5, so kappa = (0.7 - 0.5) / (1 - 0.5) = 0.40.

terms.definition: A thesis that changes because a guard dropped a clean row of its input: the guard's side effect on items that were never attacked.
The range of values the data are consistent with, at a stated confidence such as 95%. An interval that straddles 0 means no difference was detected.

Choosing what goes into the model's context window, and in what order, because every token competes for the model's attention. Week 5 measures it with an ablation that hides one block of the prompt at a time.
The automated gate that runs the tests on every change before it is merged. Written CI gate in the track; bare CI in the statistics passages means confidence interval.
A model that reads the query and one passage together and scores the pair. It is slower than comparing two vectors, so it only reorders the top hits of a faster retriever.

Lists of numbers (vectors) that a model computes from text, so that texts with similar meanings get vectors that point the same way. Retrieval with them finds paraphrases that BM25's word matching misses.
In a paired yes/no comparison, the items where the two arms disagree: one passes, the other fails. Only they say which arm is better, and McNemar's test is built on them.
terms.example: Of 60 items, 50 pass under both arms and 2 fail under both; the other 8 are discordant, 6 won by arm B and 2 by arm A.

terms.definition: A family of features: the close's distance from the indicator or level <name>, in ATRs. Positive means the close is above it, negative below.
terms.example: dist_sma_50_atr < 0 means the close sits below its 50-day average.

terms.definition: The close's distance from its 200-day simple moving average (sma_200), measured in ATRs: (close - sma_200) / ATR. It says how stretched the price is from its long-run trend, on a scale that works for any stock.
terms.example: Close 110, sma_200 100, ATR 4: dist_sma_200_atr = (110 - 100) / 4 = 2.5, so the close is 2.5 typical daily moves above its 200-day average.

terms.definition: A model grader that is registered but refuses to score until it has been validated against hand labels.
The SEC's public database of company filings: quarterly reports (10-Q), annual reports (10-K) and event reports (8-K). The track reads fundamentals and filing text from it for free.
A gap of sessions dropped just before the cutoff between training and test data, so that no training example whose outcome is still open at the cutoff reads test-period prices.
The price at which a trade is opened. A thesis gives either a limit price or a market_open entry at the next session's open.
Earnings per share: a company's profit for a period divided by its number of shares. The track reads it from SEC filings as a fundamental.
Reading real outputs, noting what went wrong, grouping and counting the failures, and only then writing evals for the classes that matter.
US Eastern Time, the time zone of the New York exchanges. The after-close run is scheduled in ET.
A short written spec for a grader, done before any code: the failure it targets, the unit it scores, its rule, and the acceptance checks it must pass.
The claim ids a thesis lists as its support. The P2 check verifies that each one exists and is a fact traceable to the source table.

The week-3 rule for what the P1 judge sees: the claims the thesis cited and the post-trade summary that code wrote from the bars, the same lines tr label show gives you. The price bars themselves stay out, because with the whole price path the judge could grade by what happened afterwards, which the rubric forbids as hindsight.
The table of failure classes from error analysis, each with a definition, an example and its count.
A made-up ticker used in test fixtures, so a test never depends on a real company's data.
A second model the code asks when the first cannot answer, so that an outage at one provider does not stop the run. The repo asks it once, after the first model's retries are spent.
The share of clean inputs that a guard wrongly blocks. It is the price of a guard: one that stops every attack but drops many good headlines is not worth having.
The share of theses whose entry was actually reached, so the trade opened. A limit entry that the price never reaches does not fill.
Further training of a model's weights on your own examples. The track treats it as the last resort, after prompts, context and checks.
Numbers from a company's financial reports, such as revenue, net income and earnings per share. The track reads them from SEC filings.
Code that scores one output, or one whole run, against a written rule, registered under an id so an experiment config can name it.

Checks around a model, not inside it: code that looks at what goes in and what comes out, and blocks or records whatever breaks a rule. Week 7's guards check the headlines before the model reads them.
The ticker of Home Depot. One of the ten stocks in the track's recorded runs; the chapters' tables and lab outputs use it as a row label.
A price band where unusually many shares changed hands over a recent period. Prices tend to pause or turn there, so the track counts each one as a level (level_hvn_1, level_hvn_2, ...).
The highest price of the prior 20 sessions, excluding today; low_20 is the lowest. Together they mark the edges of the recent range, and both count as levels.
terms.example: KO closed at 99.25 with high_20 at 98.38. The close can sit above high_20 because today is not in its window.

terms.definition: How long a thesis may stay open, counted in sessions after the fill: day (closes the same session), short (2 to 5 sessions) or swing (5 to 20 sessions). Scorecards are reported per horizon, never pooled.
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: the built-in Kubernetes controller that adds or removes copies of a service as a metric such as CPU load changes.
The price at which the thesis says its idea was wrong. P3 checks that it can be reached before the stop.
A random part added to the wait before a retry, so that clients that failed together do not all retry at the same moment. With full jitter the wait is a random time between 0 and the backoff limit.
terms.example: Before retry 3 the limit is min(30, 2**3) = 8 seconds, so the wait is a random time between 0 and 8 seconds.

terms.definition: The ticker of JPMorgan Chase. One of the ten stocks in the track's recorded runs; the chapters' tables and lab outputs use it as a row label.

The frame file that wraps the P1 rubric (evals/rubrics/p1_judge_prompt.txt, written in week 2): what the judge decides, what its INPUT and OUTPUT blocks hold, and the place where the rubric goes. For P1, INPUT is the evidence and OUTPUT is the thesis, one labelled line each for prediction, reason and invalidation text.

The theses a tr grade --judge run takes: champion and challenger theses that have a Grade and no verdict yet, oldest first. Teacher theses never wait, a thesis is never judged twice, and when the run cap runs out the newest theses are the ones left for the next run.
Checking an LLM judge before trusting it: you label a sample by hand, without seeing the judge's verdicts, and measure how well you agree, usually with Cohen's kappa.
Kubernetes event-driven autoscaling: scales a service on outside signals such as queue length, which suits model servers better than CPU load.
The ticker of Coca-Cola. One of the ten stocks in the track's recorded runs; the chapters' tables and lab outputs use it as a row label.
The memory a served language model keeps of the attention keys and values for the text so far, so it does not recompute them for each new token. It grows with context length and batch size.

The three things that together turn a prompt injection into a theft of data: an agent with access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to send data out. Remove any one and an injection can mislead but not steal.
A price the market has turned at before: a high-volume node, a pivot high or low, or the 20-day high or low. Stops and targets are placed against levels.
An order to buy or sell only at a stated price (the limit price) or better. A limit entry fills only if the price reaches it.
Large language model: a model trained on large amounts of text that writes text in reply to a prompt.
A second model call that grades an output against a written rubric, for qualities code cannot check. Its verdicts count only after they are validated against hand labels.
A trade that profits if the price rises: entry below the target, stop below the entry. A short is the mirror image.
Maximum adverse excursion: the furthest a trade moved against you before it closed, in R. It shows how close a trade came to its stop.
A label for the state of the whole market, computed from SPY (a fund that tracks the S&P 500 index), such as bull-high, where bull means a rising market. It is the regime_spy row of the source table.
An entry at the next session's open, with no price known when the thesis is written. Checks use the snapshot's last close (the reference close) in its place.
A test for a pass/fail metric on paired items: it looks only at the items where the two arms disagree and asks whether one side wins those more often than chance.
Model Context Protocol: an open protocol for exposing tools and data to a model through a server, so any compatible client can use them.
Maximum favourable excursion: the furthest a trade moved in your favour before it closed, in R. A large MFE on a losing trade means profit was given back.

Ways to split a model or its work across GPUs: tensor (TP: split each layer), pipeline (PP: split the layers), data (DP: copy the model, split the requests) and expert parallelism (EP: for a model built from many expert sub-networks, put different experts on different GPUs).
Sending each request to a model that fits it: a cheap model where it is good enough and a strong one where it is not.
The ticker of Microsoft. One of the ten stocks in the track's recorded runs; the chapters' tables and lab outputs use it as a row label.
The amount of change you see with no signal at all. In week 7 it is the share of theses that come out different when the same clean inputs run again; an attack's effect means something only above it.
A test of whether a new arm is worse than the old one by no more than a margin fixed in advance. It passes only when the whole confidence interval of the difference stays above minus the margin.
terms.example: Margin 0.02: an interval from -0.015 to +0.03 passes; one from -0.04 to +0.03 does not.

terms.definition: The ticker of Nvidia. One of the ten stocks in the track's recorded runs; the chapters' tables and lab outputs use it as a row label.
The New York Stock Exchange. Its trading calendar sets which days are sessions.

The week-3 rule that the one paid step of tr grade, the P1 judge, runs only when asked with --judge. Plain tr grade never calls a model; tr grade --judge prints what each call cost and the run's total, and --dry-run lists what it would judge and calls nothing.
The first step of error analysis: notes on each failing output in your own words, before any categories exist.
The process check that asks whether the mechanism in a thesis's reason actually happened. Code cannot read that, so an LLM judge answers met, not met or unknown.
The process check that asks whether a thesis's evidence is real: every cited fact traces to the source table.
The process check that asks whether the invalidation can be reached before the stop: stop <= invalidation < entry for a long, the mirror for a short.
The process check that asks whether stop and target are placed against the levels: the stop beyond the nearest level, the target no further than the next level plus the ATR allowance.
The 95th percentile: the value 95% of measurements fall at or below, such as a latency that only 1 call in 20 exceeds. p50 is the median.
Comparing two arms item by item on the same items, so the differences between items cancel out and a smaller sample can show an effect.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: training a small set of extra weights (for example LoRA adapters) instead of the whole model, so it fits on one GPU.
Personally identifiable information: data that can identify a person, such as a name, email or account number. It must not leak into logs or outputs.
A pivot high is a bar whose high is above the bars around it; a pivot low is a bar whose low is below them. They mark prices where the market turned, so they count as levels.

The table tr learn prints: the graded, closed champion theses, one row per horizon and setup type, never pooled. Rows with fewer than 5 trades are marked thin, because a rate from so few trades misleads.
Power is the chance a test detects a real effect of a given size; the minimum detectable effect (MDE) is the smallest effect a sample this size would detect at 80% power.
Writing down the primary metric, the guard metric and the decision rule before seeing the results, so the data cannot both suggest a rule and confirm it.
A pure function that grades how a thesis was made, before the market answers, rather than how the trade ended.

The provider keeps the processed form of a fixed prompt prefix for a few minutes, so a later request that starts with the same prefix is read from the cache at a lower price. Writing the cache costs extra.
Text in the model's input (a headline, a filing) that tries to override its instructions. Week 7 measures it and adds guards against it.
A prompt kept as its own numbered file in git (analyze-1, analyze-2), so every run records exactly which text it used.
A trade's result measured in units of its initial risk R, the distance from entry to stop. r_net is that result after the modelled trading costs.
terms.example: Entry 100, stop 95 (R = 5): closing at 110 is +2 R, hitting the stop is -1 R.

terms.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant passages first, then give them to the model with the question so its answer can cite them.
A set of metrics for retrieval-augmented answers, such as faithfulness, that can run without hand labels.
The share of the relevant passages that appear in a retriever's top k results.

Keeping secrets and personal data out of what you store, such as an API key in a trace. In the track it is structural: the code never puts them in the record, instead of scrubbing the text afterwards.

A deliberate no in place of an answer, a call or a result. A model can refuse a request; this repo records that as the answer and never sends it to a fallback model (weeks 7-8). A budget refuses a call it cannot afford with BudgetExceeded, so nothing is sent. A command refuses input it should not act on and says why. In the week-3 labs, p1_judge refuses a teacher thesis or one tr grade has not graded, raising CannotGrade before any request: no call, no run file, $0.
The table from grader id to grader class (evals.GRADERS) that the @grader decorator fills and experiment configs read.
Relative volume: the session's traded volume divided by its recent average. 1.8 means 80% more shares traded than usual, which can confirm a breakout.

A model reply recorded once and served back to every request by a swapped HTTP transport, so a lab runs offline at $0. It cannot react to what you send (it says pass to an empty prompt too), so it is evidence about your code only when your request equals the one that produced it.
Reciprocal rank fusion: combine several ranked lists by summing 1 / (k + rank) for each passage, so a passage near the top of either list rises.
Relative strength index: a 0 to 100 score of recent up moves against down moves over 14 sessions. Readings above 70 are often called overbought and below 30 oversold.
When an event happened 0 times in n tries, its true rate could still be as high as about 3/n, at 95% confidence.
terms.example: 0 clean headlines flagged in 61: the true rate of false flags could still be up to about 3/61, about 5%.

terms.definition: One dollar cap for a whole tr grade --judge run ($0.25), not one per call. Each thesis is charged what its call's run file says it spent, a reply with no verdict included. When the call budget refuses the next call, that thesis and every later one wait for the next run.

The file a run writes under data_dir/runs, holding each prompt and reply as sent and, in its header, what the calls cost. It is the only record of what a call cost: tr usage reads it, and a failed call gets one too, so a call with no run file was paid for and never counted.
A one-page statement of a system's user, job, what is out of scope, and its quality and cost bars.

The stored form of a grader's Score: the grader's id and version, the judge model, the prompt's sha256, the sample's trace and the ids of its model spans, so a stored verdict leads back to the call that made it. In week 3 the record and its verdict row are written in one transaction, or neither is and the thesis is judged again next run.
The US Securities and Exchange Commission, which receives public companies' filings.
One trading day of the exchange, from the open to the close. Horizons, embargoes and pairs are counted in sessions.
The named pattern a thesis trades, such as breakout_20d. The playbook reports results per horizon and setup type.
A simple rule-based trade opened at the same entry as each thesis, to show whether the model's choices beat a mechanical one. Real minus shadow is the difference in R.
A trade that profits if the price falls: entry above the target, stop above the entry. Also the name of a horizon, 2 to 5 sessions.
The average close over the last N sessions, written sma_N: sma_20, sma_50 and sma_200 are the 20-, 50- and 200-day averages. A close above its average suggests an uptrend over that window.
terms.example: Closes of 10, 11 and 12 give a 3-day average of 11.

terms.definition: The securities information processor feed: consolidated trades from all US exchanges. The track reads historical SIP bars from Alpaca.
Service level indicator: a number you measure about a service, such as the share of runs finished by a deadline.
Service level objective: the target you hold an SLI to, such as 99% of runs finished by 17:00 ET.
The rows of code-computed numbers (indicators, levels, fundamentals) in the model's prompt, each with a source id. A fact may cite only these rows.
The price at which a losing trade is closed, also called the stop-loss. The distance from entry to stop is the trade's risk, 1 R.
Constraining a model's reply to a schema, a fixed shape such as JSON with named fields. The schema failure rate is how often a reply still fails it.
The price at which a winning trade is closed. P4 checks that it does not sit far beyond the next level.

A model whose outputs may later train a smaller student model. In week 2, three models whose weights are public, each pinned to one provider whose terms let you keep the output, write the same analyses as the teacher arm.
The model's written trade idea for one ticker and horizon: direction, entry, stop, target, invalidation, a reason and the evidence claims. The alternative is a no-trade.
One recorded reply of the thesis model: whether it parsed, and the theses it parsed into.
A written list of who could attack a system and how, which defences cover each path, and which paths are not covered.
The short symbol a stock trades under on the exchange, such as AAPL for Apple.
One ticker on one session: the unit an analysis covers and the unit costs are compared on.
How far a fact's number may sit from its source and still match: 0.5% of the larger of the two numbers.
The model answers with a structured request, a tool name and JSON arguments, instead of text. Your code runs the tool and sends the result back, and the model goes on.
The full record of one model call or run: input, output, tool calls, tokens, cost and timing.
The ticker of UnitedHealth Group. One of the ten stocks in the track's recorded runs; the chapters' tables and lab outputs use it as a row label.

The last section of the P1 rubric: reason first, then end the reply with one JSON object on its own line, {"verdict": "pass", "explanation": "one sentence"}, with exactly those keys and the verdict in lower case. The reader takes the last JSON object in the reply, because the reasoning may quote the format example or try a draft verdict first.
A test for paired numeric differences: it ranks the per-item differences by size and checks whether the positive and negative ranks balance.
A confidence interval for a proportion, such as a win rate, that stays sensible at small n and near 0% or 100%.
The share of graded trades that closed with a profit.
The tagged data format of SEC financial statements, which lets code read a figure such as EPS without parsing prose.
The ticker of Exxon Mobil. One of the ten stocks in the track's recorded runs; the chapters' tables and lab outputs use it as a row label.
